claim: Class III myosins (Myo3) and actin-bundling protein Espin play critical roles in regulating the development and maintenance of stereocilia in vertebrate hair cells.
source: Class III myosins (Myo3) and actin-bundling protein Espin play critical roles in regulating the development and maintenance of stereocilia in vertebrate hair cells, and their defects cause hereditary hearing impairments.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established knowledge in the field and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Defects in Myo3 and Espin cause hereditary hearing impairments.
source: Class III myosins (Myo3) and actin-bundling protein Espin play critical roles in regulating the development and maintenance of stereocilia in vertebrate hair cells, and their defects cause hereditary hearing impairments.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genetic studies mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Myo3 interacts with Espin1 through its tail homology I motif (THDI).
source: Myo3 interacts with Espin1 through its tail homology I motif (THDI), however it is not clear how Myo3 specifically acts through Espin1 to regulate the actin bundle assembly and stabilization.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Myo3 THDI contains a pair of repeat sequences capable of independently and strongly binding to the ankyrin repeats of Espin1.
source: Here we discover that Myo3 THDI contains a pair of repeat sequences capable of independently and strongly binding to the ankyrin repeats of Espin1, revealing an unexpected Myo3-mediated cross-linking mechanism of Espin1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ITC binding assays and structural studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structures of Myo3 in complex with Espin1 elucidate the mechanism of the binding.
source: The structures of Myo3 in complex with Espin1 not only elucidate the mechanism of the binding, but also reveal a Myo3-induced release of Espin1 auto-inhibition mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structures determined in the study.

claim: The structures of Myo3 in complex with Espin1 reveal a Myo3-induced release of Espin1 auto-inhibition mechanism.
source: The structures of Myo3 in complex with Espin1 not only elucidate the mechanism of the binding, but also reveal a Myo3-induced release of Espin1 auto-inhibition mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Myo3-mediated cross-linking can further promote actin fiber bundling activity of Espin1.
source: We also provide evidence that Myo3-mediated cross-linking can further promote actin fiber bundling activity of Espin1.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence and electron microscopy data showing thicker actin bundles in the presence of Myo3-ARB12.

claim: The first member of Myo3 was identified in Drosophila photoreceptors and named as NinaC.
source: The first member of Myo3 was identified in Drosophila photoreceptors and named as NinaC (neither inactivation nor afterpotential C) (Montell and Rubin, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Montell and Rubin, 1988.

claim: There are two paralogs of Myo3 in vertebrate, Myo3a and Myo3b.
source: There are two paralogs of Myo3 in vertebrate, Myo3a and Myo3b, both of which are known to express in vertebrate retina and cochlea (Dose and Burnside, 2000, 2002; Shin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Myo3a and Myo3b are known to express in vertebrate retina and cochlea.
source: There are two paralogs of Myo3 in vertebrate, Myo3a and Myo3b, both of which are known to express in vertebrate retina and cochlea (Dose and Burnside, 2000, 2002; Shin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dose and Burnside, 2000, 2002; Shin et al., 2013.

claim: Myo3a and Myo3b may play partially redundant roles as transporters that are crucial for vertebrate photoreceptor and stereocilia ultrastructure maintenance.
source: It is believed that they may play partially redundant roles as transporters that are crucial for vertebrate photoreceptor and stereocilia ultrastructure maintenance (Manor et al., 2012; Mecklenburg et al., 2015; Merritt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Manor et al., 2012; Mecklenburg et al., 2015; Merritt et al., 2012.

claim: Myo3 across different species all contain an N-terminal S/T kinase domain before their motor head.
source: Myo3 across different species all contain an N-terminal S/T kinase domain before their motor head.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Myo3 structure.

claim: The kinase domain has been reported to regulate the motor's ATPase activity.
source: The kinase domain has been reported to regulate the motor's ATPase activity (Komaba et al., 2010; Quintero et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Komaba et al., 2010; Quintero et al., 2010.

claim: The tail regions of Myo3 from different species are less conserved.
source: The tail regions of Myo3 from different species are less conserved.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis and established knowledge.

claim: Drosophila NinaC contains a PDZ binding motif at its very C-terminus capable of binding to a master scaffold protein called INAD.
source: Drosophila NinaC contains a PDZ binding motif at its very C-terminus capable of binding to a master scaffold protein called INAD (Inactivation no afterpotential D) (Wes et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wes et al., 1999.

claim: Vertebrate Myo3 tails share a conserved vertebrate specific domain referred to as tail homology I motif (THDI).
source: Vertebrate Myo3 tails share a conserved vertebrate specific domain referred to as tail homology I motif (THDI) (Figure 1A) (Dose et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dose et al., 2003 and Figure 1A showing domain organization.

claim: Once tip localized, Espin1 WH2 domain promotes the elongation of actin protrusions.
source: Once tip localized, Espin1 WH2 domain promotes the elongation of actin protrusions (Merritt et al., 2012; Salles et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Merritt et al., 2012; Salles et al., 2009.

claim: Espin1 was first identified in Sertoli cell-spermatid junctions.
source: Espin1 was first identified in Sertoli cell-spermatid junctions (Bartles et al., 1996), encoded by the gene Espin.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bartles et al., 1996.

claim: Shorter spliced isoforms of Espin gene products (Espin2B, Espin3A and Espin4) were shown to be expressed in other F-actin rich structures such as brush border microvilli and Purkinje cell dendritic spines.
source: Later, shorter spliced isoforms of Espin gene products (Espin2B, Espin3A and Espin4) were shown to be expressed in other F-actin rich structures such as brush border microvilli and Purkinje cell dendritic spines (Bartles et al., 1998; Sekerkova et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bartles et al., 1998; Sekerkova et al., 2003.

claim: All Espin isoforms share a common 14 kDa C-terminal actin binding domain (ABD).
source: They share a common 14 kDa C-terminal actin binding domain (ABD; Figure 1A), which was reported to be necessary and sufficient for F-actin bundling activity (Bartles, 2000; Bartles et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and Figure 1A showing domain organization.

claim: The ABD of Espin was reported to be necessary and sufficient for F-actin bundling activity.
source: They share a common 14 kDa C-terminal actin binding domain (ABD; Figure 1A), which was reported to be necessary and sufficient for F-actin bundling activity (Bartles, 2000; Bartles et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bartles, 2000; Bartles et al., 1998.

claim: All Espin isoforms contain a WH2 motif which can bind to actin monomer.
source: Besides the ABD, all Espin isoforms contain a WH2 motif which can bind to actin monomer and a proline rich (PR) region which can interact with profilins (Sekerkova et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sekerkova et al., 2006.

claim: All Espin isoforms contain a proline rich (PR) region which can interact with profilins.
source: Besides the ABD, all Espin isoforms contain a WH2 motif which can bind to actin monomer and a proline rich (PR) region which can interact with profilins (Sekerkova et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sekerkova et al., 2006.

claim: Espin2B contains one more PR region and an extra actin binding site (xAB) at the N-terminus.
source: Espin2B contains one more PR region and an extra actin binding site (xAB) at the N-terminus (Chen et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 1999.

claim: Espin1 is the longest isoform in the family and contains a stretch of ankyrin repeats (AR) in its N-terminus.
source: Espin1 is the longest isoform in the family and contains a stretch of ankyrin repeats (AR) in its N-terminus (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A showing domain organization.

claim: The AR of Espin1 is responsible for directly interacting with Myo3 tail THDI.
source: The AR of Espin1 is responsible for directly interacting with Myo3 tail THDI (Merritt et al., 2012; Salles et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Merritt et al., 2012; Salles et al., 2009.

claim: Espin1 contains an AR binding sequence immediately C-terminal to xAB, and binding of AR to this sequence prevents xAB from binding to actin.
source: Recently, it was reported that Espin1 contains an AR binding sequence immediately C-terminal to xAB, and binding of AR to this sequence prevents xAB from binding to actin (Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zheng et al., 2014.

claim: The actin binding activity of the N-terminal part of Espin1 is auto-inhibited.
source: As such, the actin binding activity of the N-terminal part of Espin1 is auto-inhibited, and this AR-binding region is named as the auto-inhibitory region (AI, Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the binding of AR to the AI region and citation to Zheng et al., 2014.

claim: Myo3 binding can release the auto-inhibition and increase the diameter of Espin1-promoted actin bundles.
source: The authors also proposed that Myo3 binding can release the auto-inhibition and increase the diameter of Espin1-promoted actin bundles (Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zheng et al., 2014.

claim: Myo3a/Myo3b are known to co-localize with Espin1 at the tips of stereocilia of hair cells.
source: Myo3a/Myo3b are known to co-localize with Espin1 at the tips of stereocilia of hair cells (Merritt et al., 2012; Salles et al., 2009; Schneider et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Merritt et al., 2012; Salles et al., 2009; Schneider et al., 2006.

claim: Co-expression of Myo3a and Espin1 can further stimulate elongation of stereocilia in cultured organ of Corti hair cells.
source: Importantly, co-expression of Myo3a and Espin1 can further stimulate elongation of stereocilia in cultured organ of Corti hair cells (Salles et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Salles et al., 2009.

claim: When expressed in heterologous cells, Myo3a gets enriched at the tip of filopodia.
source: When expressed in heterologous cells, Myo3a gets enriched at the tip of filopodia (Les Erickson et al., 2003; Salles et al., 2009; Schneider et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Les Erickson et al., 2003; Salles et al., 2009; Schneider et al., 2006.

claim: Mutations of human Myo3a gene is known to cause progressive non-syndromic hearing loss, DFNB30.
source: Mutations of human Myo3a gene is known to cause progressive non-syndromic hearing loss, DFNB30 (Walsh et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Walsh et al., 2002.

claim: Transgenic mice with DFNB30 mutation undergo age-dependent outer hair cell degeneration.
source: Also, transgenic mice with DFNB30 mutation undergo age-dependent outer hair cell degeneration (Walsh et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Walsh et al., 2011.

claim: The jerker mouse carrying espin frame-shift mutation suffers from hair cells degeneration, deafness and vestibular dysfunction.
source: The jerker mouse carrying espin frame-shift mutation suffers from hair cells degeneration, deafness and vestibular dysfunction (Sekerkova et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sekerkova et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2000.

claim: Mutations in espin were reported to be associated with non-syndromic autosomal recessive deafness DFNB36 and non-syndromic autosomal dominant deafness.
source: Mutations in espin were also reported to be associated with non-syndromic autosomal recessive deafness DFNB36 and non-syndromic autosomal dominant deafness (Boulouiz et al., 2008; Donaudy et al., 2006; Naz et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boulouiz et al., 2008; Donaudy et al., 2006; Naz et al., 2004.

claim: A prominent phenotype of the jerker mice is that their hair cell stereocilia are uniformly thinner and shorter, degenerate faster than those of the wild type littermates.
source: A prominent phenotype of the jerker mice is that their hair cell stereocilia are uniformly thinner and shorter, degenerate faster than those of the wild type littermates (Sekerkova et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sekerkova et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2000.

claim: Both Myo3a and Myo3b contain two highly similar repeat sequences in their THDI region, each capable of independently binding to Espin1-AR with high affinity.
source: Here, we discover that both Myo3a and Myo3b contain two highly similar repeat sequences in their THDI region, each capable of independently binding to Espin1-AR with high affinity.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The THDI region contains a pair of repeating sequences in its N- and C-terminal halves.
source: First we analyzed the sequences of the reported Espin1-binding THDI regions of both Myo3a and Myo3b, and found that the region contains a pair of repeating sequences in its N- and C-terminal halves (Figure 1A and B, denoted as ARB1 and ARB2 for Espin1 ankyrin repeats binding region 1 and 2 as detailed below).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Purified THDI from both Myo3a and Myo3b can bind to Espin1-AR with high affinities (Kd in the range of tens of nanomolars).
source: Using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC)-based quantitative binding assay, we found that purified THDI from both Myo3a and Myo3b can bind to Espin1-AR with high affinities (Kd in the range of tens of nanomolars; Figure 1C1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1C1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The binding stoichiometry of the Myo3 THDI and Espin1-AR clearly deviates from the value of 1:1.
source: Inspection of the ITC-based titration curves indicated that the binding stoichiometry of the Myo3 THDI and Espin1-AR clearly deviates from the value of 1:1 (Figure 1C1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1C1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Each of the two repeat sequences in Myo3 THDI may independently bind to Espin1-AR, forming a 2:1 stoichiometric complex.
source: We thus hypothesized that each of the two repeat sequences in Myo3 THDI may independently bind to Espin1-AR, forming a 2:1 stoichiometric complex.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on ITC data and is verified by subsequent experiments.

claim: Myo3b THDI is saturated by the binding of two molar ratios Espin1-AR.
source: However, further addition of Espin1-AR did not change the elution volume of the complex any more, indicating that Myo3b THDI is saturated by the binding of two molar ratios Espin1-AR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The fitted molecular weight of the Myo3b THDI and Espin1-AR complex (~109.5 kDa) matches well with the theoretical molecular weight of 117 kDa for the (Trx-Espin1-AR)2/Myo3b-THDI complex.
source: When mixed Myo3b THDI with saturated amount of Trx-tagged Espin1-AR, the fitted molecular weight of the complex peak (~109.5 kDa) matches well with the theoretical molecular weight of 117 kDa for the (Trx-Espin1-AR)2/Myo3b-THDI complex (Figure 1D), confirming that Myo3 THDI contains two Espin1-AR binding sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by FPLC-MALS data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both Myo3 ARB1 and ARB2 bind to Espin1-AR with affinities also in the range of tens of nanomolars and each with a 1:1 stoichiometry.
source: Both Myo3 ARB1 and ARB2 bind to Espin1-AR with affinities also in the range of tens of nanomolars and each with a 1:1 stoichiometry (Figure 1C2 and 1C3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C), indicating that the two repeating sequences in Myo3-THDI can independently bind to Espin1-AR with comparable affinities.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1C2, 1C3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The 1:2 stoichiometry between Myo3 and Espin1 is consistent with a previous finding that human Myo3a THDI lacking exon 33 can still interact with Espin1.
source: The 1:2 stoichiometry between Myo3 and Espin1 is consistent with a previous finding that human Myo3a THDI lacking exon 33 (exon 33 mainly encodes ARB2) can still interact with Espin1 (Salles et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Salles et al., 2009 and the current study's data.

claim: The crystal structure of the Espin1-AR/Myo3b-ARB1 complex was solved at 1.65 Å resolution.
source: To understand the molecular basis of the Espin1/Myo3 interaction, we solved the crystal structure of the Espin1-AR/Myo3b-ARB1 complex at 1.65 Å resolution (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: Espin1-AR contains 10 ANK repeats.
source: The structure revealed that Espin1-AR contains 10 ANK repeats (Figure 2), instead of 8 as predicted earlier (Bartles et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: The repeats 2–9 of Espin1-AR each contains the signature 'TPLH' sequence at the N-terminus of the αA helix.
source: The repeats 2–9 each contains the signature 'TPLH' sequence at the N-terminus of the αA helix, so can be viewed as the canonical ANK repeats.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two ANK repeats capping the two termini of Espin1-AR do not contain the 'TPLH' sequence.
source: Like shown in the recently determined structures of the 24 ANK repeats scaffold protein ankyrin-B (Wang et al., 2014) and the 9 ANK repeats RNase L (Han et al., 2012), the two ANK repeats capping the two termini of Espin1-AR do not contain the 'TPLH' sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison and sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two non-canonical ANK repeats capping the two termini of Espin1-AR mainly play a structural stabilization role of the entire AR fold.
source: We believe that these two non-canonical ANK repeats capping the two termini of Espin1-AR mainly play a structural stabilization role of the entire AR fold.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural analysis and comparison with other ANK repeat proteins.

claim: The 10 ANK repeats form a left-handed superhelix with the αA helices forming the inner groove and the αB helices forming the outer surface.
source: The 10 ANK repeats form a left-handed superhelix with the αA helices forming the inner groove and the αB helices forming the outer surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ARB1 binds to Espin1-AR in an antiparallel manner.
source: The ARB1 binds to Espin1-AR in an antiparallel manner, similar to the binding mode between ANK repeats from Ankyrin R/B/G and their targets (Wang et al., 2014) as well as between ANKRA2/RFXANK and their targets (Xu et al., 2012), suggesting that elongated inner grooves are common target binding sites of ANK repeats in general.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and comparison with other ANK repeat complexes.

claim: The ARB1 spans nearly the entire inner groove, covering ~1230 Å2 of solvent accessible area.
source: The ARB1 spans nearly the entire inner groove, covering ~1230 Å2 of solvent accessible area.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the complex.

claim: The N-terminal of ARB1 adopts an extended structure and binds to the C-terminal of Espin1-AR.
source: The N-terminal of ARB1 adopts an extended structure and binds to the C-terminal of Espin1-AR.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The C-terminal of ARB1 forms an α-helix and binds to the N-terminal half of Espin1-AR.
source: The C-terminal of ARB1 forms an α-helix and binds to the N-terminal half of Espin1-AR (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The amino acid sequences of Espin1-AR from different vertebrate species as well as of the mammalian paralogs Espin-like proteins are highly conserved.
source: The amino acid sequences of Espin1-AR from different vertebrate species as well as of the mammalian paralogs Espin-like proteins (Shin et al., 2013) are highly conserved (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The residues in the inner groove of AR are highly conserved.
source: We mapped the sequence conservation profile to the structure of Espin1-AR and found that the residues in the inner groove of AR are highly conserved.
evidence: This claim is supported by conservation mapping shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The residues in the ARB1 binding surface are essentially totally conserved.
source: In particular the residues in the ARB1 binding surface are essentially totally conserved (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by conservation mapping shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The structure of the Espin1-AR/Myo3b-ARB2 complex was determined at a resolution of 2.3 Å.
source: We have also determined the Espin1-AR/Myo3b-ARB2 complex at a resolution of 2.3 Å (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: The structure of the Espin1-AR/Myo3b-ARB2 complex and the binding mode of Myo3b-ARB2 to Espin1-AR are highly similar to what are observed in the Espin1-AR/Myo3b-ARB1 complex.
source: The structure of the complex and the binding mode of Myo3b-ARB2 to Espin1-AR are highly similar to what are observed in the Espin1-AR/Myo3b-ARB1 complex (Figure 2D), directly confirming our earlier conclusion that the two repeat sequences in Myo3-THDI bind to Espin1-AR with similar binding mode and affinity.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Two absolutely conserved tyrosine residues (Tyr1267ARB1 and Tyr1268ARB1) and Leu1271ARB1 in ARB1 insert into the hydrophobic pocket in the N-terminal of Espin1-AR.
source: Two absolutely conserved tyrosine residues (Tyr1267ARB1 and Tyr1268ARB1, the double tyrosine ('YY') motif; Figure 3B) and Leu1271ARB1 in the next turn insert into the hydrophobic pocket in the N-terminal of Espin1-AR (Figure 3A1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3A1.

claim: Mutations of the two tyrosine residues (Tyr1267 and Tyr1268) to alanine greatly decreased Myo3b-ARB1's binding to Espin1-AR.
source: Mutations of these two tyrosine residues to alanine greatly decreased Myo3b-ARB1's binding to Espin1-AR (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mutation of Leu110 in the Espin1-AR hydrophobic pocket to aspartic acid decreased the affinity by ~10-fold.
source: Similarly, mutation of Leu110 in the Espin1-AR hydrophobic pocket to a polar residue aspartic acid decreased the affinity by ~10-fold (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mutation of Asp1264ARB1 together with Glu1263ARB1 to alanines decreased the affinity by ~10-fold.
source: Furthermore, the carboxyl group of Asp1264ARB1 makes hydrogen bonds with Asn69 and Ser103. Mutation of this residue together with Glu1263ARB1 to alanines decreased the affinity by ~10-fold (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mutation of Lys1257ARB1 to glutamic acid, together with Leu1259ARB1 to alanine substitution decreased the affinity by about ~10-fold.
source: Mutation of Lys1257ARB1 into a reversed charged residue glutamic acid, together with Leu1259ARB1 to alanine substitution also decreased the affinity by about ~10-fold (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mutating Arg1251ARB1 and Arg1252ARB1 to glutamic acid decreased Myo3B-ARB1 binding to Espin1-AR by ~15-fold.
source: Mutating these two arginine residues to reverse charged residues glutamic acid decreased Myo3B-ARB1 binding to Espin1-AR by ~15-fold (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Substitutions of Arg1282ARB2 and Lys1283ARB2 with alanines decreased Myo3b-ARB2 binding to Espin1-AR by ~10-fold.
source: Indeed, substitutions of the more N-terminal positively charged residues of Myo3b-ARB2 (Arg1282ARB2 and Lys1283ARB2) with alanines decreased its binding to Espin1-AR by ~10-fold (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Espin1-AI bears high sequence homology with Myo3-ARBs.
source: By comparing the sequence of AI (aa 496–529) with the consensus sequence of Myo3-ARBs, we find that Espin1-AI bears high sequence homology with Myo3-ARBs (e.g. the completely conserved 'YY' motif, the central 'KxL' motif, and the N-terminal positively charged residues; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Espin1-AI can bind to Espin1-AR with a Kd of 1.32 μM.
source: We used ITC-based binding assay to test this prediction, and found that Espin1-AI can indeed bind to Espin1-AR, albeit with a more moderate affinity than Myo3-ARBs (Kd of 1.32 μM vs 0.05~0.1 μM) (Figure 4C1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4C1.

claim: Substitutions of the two tyrosines in Espin1-AI to alanines greatly weakened its binding to Espin1-AR.
source: Fully consistent with our structure-based sequence alignment analysis, substitutions of the two tyrosines in Espin1-AI to alanines greatly weakened its binding to Espin1-AR (Figure 4C2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4C2.

claim: The interaction between Espin1 AR and AI can conformationally mask the xAB's actin binding activity and thus renders Espin1 in an auto-inhibited conformation.
source: Given that the AI segment (aa 496–529) is immediately C-terminal to xAB (aa 462–487) of Espin1 (Figure 4A), one might envision that the interaction between Espin1 AR and AI can conformationally mask the xAB's actin binding activity and thus renders Espin1 in an auto-inhibited conformation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural and biochemical data.

claim: Myo3a-ARB1 can bind to Espin1-1-529 with a sub-micromolar affinity.
source: ITC-based assay further showed that Myo3a-ARB1 can indeed bind to both Espin1-1-529 and Espin1-FL and with a weaker binding affinity than binding to Espin1-AR (Figure 4D1–3), consistent with a partially blocked Espin1-AR binding groove by AI.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4D1.

claim: Myo3a-ARB1 can bind to Espin1-FL with a sub-micromolar affinity.
source: ITC-based assay further showed that Myo3a-ARB1 can indeed bind to both Espin1-1-529 and Espin1-FL and with a weaker binding affinity than binding to Espin1-AR (Figure 4D1–3), consistent with a partially blocked Espin1-AR binding groove by AI.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4D2.

claim: Myo3a-ARB1 binds to Espin1-1-529 and Espin1-FL with a weaker binding affinity than binding to Espin1-AR.
source: ITC-based assay further showed that Myo3a-ARB1 can indeed bind to both Espin1-1-529 and Espin1-FL and with a weaker binding affinity than binding to Espin1-AR (Figure 4D1–3), consistent with a partially blocked Espin1-AR binding groove by AI.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4D1-3.

claim: Both Espin1-1-529 and Espin1-FL exist as monomer in solution.
source: We obtained highly purified N-terminal auto-inhibitory fragment of Espin1 spanning from AR to AI (denoted as Espin1-1-529, Figure 4A) and the full length Espin1 (denoted as Espin1-FL), and found that both proteins exist as monomer in solution (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that Espin1 auto-inhibition is intra-molecular in nature.
evidence: This claim is supported by FPLC-SLS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Espin1 auto-inhibition is intra-molecular in nature.
source: We obtained highly purified N-terminal auto-inhibitory fragment of Espin1 spanning from AR to AI (denoted as Espin1-1-529, Figure 4A) and the full length Espin1 (denoted as Espin1-FL), and found that both proteins exist as monomer in solution (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that Espin1 auto-inhibition is intra-molecular in nature.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from FPLC-SLS data showing monomeric state.

claim: The ITC titration reactions of Myo3a-ARB1 to Espin1-1-529 and Espin1-FL are endothermic instead of exothermic.
source: We also noticed that the ITC titration reactions of Myo3a-ARB1 to Espin1-1-529 and Espin1-FL are endothermic (Figure 4D1 and 4D2) instead of the exothermic reactions between Myo3a-ARB1 titrating to Espin1-AR (Figure 4D3), further indicating that the binding of Myo3a-ARB1 to the auto-inhibited Espin1 is not a simple direct association process between ARB1 and AR.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4D1, 4D2, and 4D3.

claim: Espin1-1-494 binds to Myo3a-ARB1 with an affinity similar to that between Espin1-AR and Myo3a-ARB1.
source: To provide further proof, we truncated Espin1 from the C-terminus just before the AI (i.e., aa 1–494, denoted as Espin1-1-494) and found that Espin1-1-494 binds to Myo3a-ARB1 with an affinity similar to that between Espin1-AR and Myo3a-ARB1 (Figure 4D3), indicating that AI is indeed responsible for the decreased binding of Espin1 to Myo3a-ARB1.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4D4.

claim: AI is responsible for the decreased binding of Espin1 to Myo3a-ARB1.
source: To provide further proof, we truncated Espin1 from the C-terminus just before the AI (i.e., aa 1–494, denoted as Espin1-1-494) and found that Espin1-1-494 binds to Myo3a-ARB1 with an affinity similar to that between Espin1-AR and Myo3a-ARB1 (Figure 4D3), indicating that AI is indeed responsible for the decreased binding of Espin1 to Myo3a-ARB1.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from ITC data comparing binding affinities.

claim: Myo3a is known to localize at the tip of filopodia when transfected in heterologous cells like HeLa or COS7 cells.
source: Myo3a is known to localize at the tip of filopodia when transfected in heterologous cells like HeLa or COS7 cells, whereas Myo3b alone cannot tip-localize as it lacks ABM (Les Erickson et al., 2003; Salles et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Les Erickson et al., 2003; Salles et al., 2009.

claim: Myo3b alone cannot tip-localize as it lacks ABM.
source: Myo3a is known to localize at the tip of filopodia when transfected in heterologous cells like HeLa or COS7 cells, whereas Myo3b alone cannot tip-localize as it lacks ABM (Les Erickson et al., 2003; Salles et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Les Erickson et al., 2003; Salles et al., 2009.

claim: When co-expressed with Espin1, Myo3b can bind to Espin1 and localize to the tip of filopodia.
source: However, when co-expressed with Espin1, Myo3b can bind to Espin1 and localize to the tip of filopodia (Manor et al., 2012; Merritt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Manor et al., 2012; Merritt et al., 2012.

claim: Myo3a lacking ABM can only tip-localize when co-expressed with Espin1.
source: Similarly, Myo3a lacking ABM can only tip-localize when co-expressed with Espin1.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the role of Espin1 binding in tip localization.

claim: Deletion of the Myo3 kinase domain is known to render the motor in a constant active state in promoting the length of filopodia.
source: Deletion of the Myo3 kinase domain is known to render the motor in a constant active state in promoting the length of filopodia, thus we used Myo3 constructs lacking the kinase domain in the subsequent experiments (Les Erickson et al., 2003; Quintero et al., 2010; 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Les Erickson et al., 2003; Quintero et al., 2010; 2013.

claim: Both GFP-tagged wild type Myo3a (lacking the kinase domain and the ABM) and RFP-tagged Espin1 localized to the tip of filopodia when co-transfected in COS7 cells.
source: As expected, both GFP-tagged wild type Myo3a (lacking the kinase domain and the ABM, denoted as ΔKΔABM) and RFP-tagged Espin1 localized to the tip of filopodia when co-transfected in COS7 cells (Figure 5A1).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A1.

claim: Mutation of the 'YY' motif of either of the ARBs only had a moderate or even unobservable effect on filopodia tip localization for both Myo3a and Espin1.
source: Mutation of the 'YY' motif of either of the ARBs (denoted as mARB1 and mARB2) only had a moderate or even unobservable effect on filopodia tip localization for both Myo3a and Espin1 (Figure 5B), indicating that ARB1 and ARB2 may play some redundant functions in this overexpression system.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ARB1 and ARB2 may play some redundant functions in the overexpression system.
source: Mutation of the 'YY' motif of either of the ARBs (denoted as mARB1 and mARB2) only had a moderate or even unobservable effect on filopodia tip localization for both Myo3a and Espin1 (Figure 5B), indicating that ARB1 and ARB2 may play some redundant functions in this overexpression system.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the moderate effect of single ARB mutations.

claim: Mutations of both 'YY' motifs significantly reduced the filopodia tip localization of Myo3a.
source: Mutations of both 'YY' motifs (mARB1+mARB2, denoted as mARB) significantly reduced the filopodia tip localization of Myo3a (Figure 5A2 and Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 5A2 and 5B.

claim: Deletion of one ARB had a moderate effect and deletion of both ARBs had a much more severe effect on filopodia tip localization of Myo3a.
source: Similarly, deletion of one ARB had a moderate effect and deletion of both ARBs had a much more severe effect on filopodia tip localization of Myo3a (Figure 5A3 and Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 5A3 and 5B.

claim: The ratio of tip to cell body protein level of Myo3b is significantly less than that of Myo3a.
source: It is worth noting that the ratio of tip to cell body protein level of Myo3b is significantly less than that of Myo3a (Figure 5B and C), which is also consistent with previously reported findings (Manor et al., 2012; Merritt et al., 2012), but the detailed mechanism for this difference is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B and 5C and citations to prior studies.

claim: Both ARBs in Myo3a or Myo3b are important for filopodia tip localizations of Myo3 and Espin1.
source: The above results demonstrate that both ARBs in Myo3a or Myo3b are important for filopodia tip localizations of Myo3 and Espin1.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cell-based localization experiments.

claim: Under FM, the F-actin alone showed only background signal when probed by fluorescence-labeled phalloidin since individual F-actin is too small to be resolved.
source: Under FM, the F-actin alone showed only background signal when probed by fluorescence-labeled phalloidin since individual F-actin is too small to be resolved (Figure 6B, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When Espin1 was added into the F-actin solution, uniform needle like bundles could be observed under FM.
source: When Espin1 was added into the F-actin solution, uniform needle like bundles could be observed under FM.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6A1.

claim: TEM showed that the bundle size of Espin1-induced actin bundles is ~190 ± 8 nm in width.
source: TEM showed that the bundle size is ~190 ± 8 nm in width (mean ± SEM) (Figure 6A1 and C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data and quantification shown in Figure 6A1, 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: By adding ARB1 or ARB2 to Espin1 and F-actin containing solution, some of the actin bundles were cross-linked and formed clusters under FM and TEM.
source: By adding ARB1 or ARB2 to Espin1 and F-actin containing solution, some of the actin bundles were cross-linked and formed clusters under FM and TEM (Figure 6A2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence and electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6A2 and 6A3.

claim: The addition of ARBs slightly increased the width of the actin bundles, with 216 ± 9 nm for the ARB1 group and 218 ± 9 nm for the ARB2 group.
source: Quantification of the F-actin bundle width from the TEM images revealed that the addition of ARBs slightly increased the width of the actin bundles, with 216 ± 9 nm for the ARB1 group and 218 ± 9 nm for the ARB2 group (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of TEM data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When ARB12 were added to Espin1 and F-actin containing solution, significantly thicker, elongated, and less branched bundles were observed under FM.
source: Interestingly, when ARB12 were added to Espin1 and F-actin containing solution, significantly thicker, elongated, and less branched bundles were observed under FM (Figure 6A4, left), a morphology clearly distinct from that with the addition of either ARB1 alone or ARB2 alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6A4.

claim: The thicker bundles formed in the presence of ARB12 appear to be composed of several thinner actin bundles as observed in the Espin1-ABD-promoted actin bundles.
source: When examined under TEM, the thicker bundles appear to be composed of several thinner actin bundles as observed in the Espin1-ABD-promoted actin bundles (Figure 6A4, right and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), indicating that Myo3-ARB12-mediated binding of Espin1 can promote/stabilize parallel actin fiber formation presumably due to Myo3 mediated cross-linking of Espin1.
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6A4 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The average width of the actin bundles formed in the presence of Myo3-ARB12 and Espin1 are significantly larger (330 ± 20 nm) than the other three groups.
source: Quantification of the width of actin bundles formed in the presence the Myo3-ARB12 and Espin1 showed that the average width of the actin bundles are significantly larger (330 ± 20; with the thickest bundles reaching ~600 nm in width) than the other three groups (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of TEM data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Myo3a-ARB12 alone could not cause bundling of F-actin.
source: As a control, Myo3a-ARB12 alone could not cause bundling of F-actin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A key function of the Myo3/Espin1 interaction is to promote formation of thicker parallel actin bundle fibers in cellular structures such as stereocilia.
source: Therefore, one can envision that a key function of the Myo3/Espin1 interaction is to promote formation of thicker parallel actin bundle fibers in cellular structures such as stereocilia.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the actin bundling data and the known localization of Myo3 and Espin1 in stereocilia.

claim: The Myo3 binding sites in Myo3a and Myo3b are essentially identical and therefore are predicted to be functionally interchangeable.
source: We demonstrate that the Espin1 binding sites in Myo3a and Myo3b are essentially identical and therefore are predicted to be functionally interchangeable.
evidence: This claim is based on structural and biochemical data showing similar binding modes and affinities.

claim: These findings provide a molecular explanation for the partially redundant functions of Myo3a and Myo3b in hair cells.
source: These findings provide a molecular explanation for the partially redundant functions of Myo3a and Myo3b in hair cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the structural and functional data.

claim: Espin-like proteins can also bind to Myo3 as Espin1 does.
source: This analysis also predicts that Espin-like proteins can also bind to Myo3 as Espin1 does, suggesting that the functions of Espin1 and Espin-like protein may also be partially redundant in tissues like stereocilia (Shin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from sequence conservation and structural analysis.

claim: The functions of Espin1 and Espin-like protein may be partially redundant in tissues like stereocilia.
source: This analysis also predicts that Espin-like proteins can also bind to Myo3 as Espin1 does, suggesting that the functions of Espin1 and Espin-like protein may also be partially redundant in tissues like stereocilia (Shin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from sequence conservation and a citation to Shin et al., 2013.

claim: Forked, the Drosophila ortholog of Espin, is expressed in bristle cells.
source: Moreover, we note that forked, the Drosophila ortholog of Espin, is expressed in bristle cells, a cell type that is enriched in bundled actin filaments (Petersen et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Petersen et al., 1994.

claim: Drosophila Forked protein is predicted to contain five ANK repeats, corresponding to Espin1 repeats 5–9.
source: Drosophila Forked protein is predicted to contain five ANK repeats, corresponding to Espin1 repeats 5–9.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis and prediction.

claim: The different tip localization patterns of Myo3a and Myo3b does not originate from the unique ABM of Myo3a.
source: The different tip localization patterns of Myo3a and Myo3b does not originate from the unique ABM of Myo3a (Manor et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Manor et al., 2012.

claim: The Espin1 binding THDI regions of Myo3a and Myo3b are not responsible for different localizations of Myo3a and Myo3b along stereocilia/filopodia.
source: Our study here suggests that their Espin1 binding THDI regions are not responsible for different localizations of Myo3a and Myo3b along stereocilia/filopodia either.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current study's findings.

claim: The kinetics and the F-actin binding affinities of the motor domains or other variable regions in the tails of Myo3a and Myo3b may contribute to their different localizations.
source: It is possible that the kinetics and the F-actin binding affinities of their motor domains or other variable regions in their tails may contribute to such differences.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing possible mechanisms for observed differences.

claim: Most of the unconventional myosins use their globular cargo binding domains to recognize their cargoes.
source: Most of the unconventional myosins use their globular cargo binding domains to recognize their cargoes (Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2014.

claim: Myo3 use their unstructured, yet highly conserved tails to recognize globular domains from their cargoes.
source: However, Myo3 use their unstructured, yet highly conserved tails to recognize globular domains from their cargoes.
evidence: This claim is based on the structural and biochemical findings of the current study.

claim: Myo3 and Myosin XIX are not predicted to contain folded globular domains in their tail regions.
source: Myo3 and another unconventional myosins, Myosin XIX, are not predicted to contain folded globular domains in their tail regions (Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2014.

claim: Another region in Myo3a's tail, which is located immediately N-terminal to the Espin1 binding ARB12 region, can bind to MORN4.
source: A very recent report showed that another region in Myo3a's tail, which is located immediately N-terminal to the Espin1 binding ARB12 region, can bind to MORN4 (Mecklenburg et al., 2015), the mammalian ortholog of Drosophila Retinophilin.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mecklenburg et al., 2015.

claim: Retinophilin can bind to Drosophila NinaC.
source: It is noted that Retinophilin can also bind to Drosophila NinaC (Venkatachalam et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Venkatachalam et al., 2010.

claim: Stereocilia in jerker mice are thinner in their diameters likely due to loss of Espin1-mediated higher order actin fiber assembly.
source: Fitting with this model, stereocilia in jerker mice are thinner in their diameters likely due to loss of Espin1-mediated higher order actin fiber assembly, easier to form tapered structures and easier to degenerate presumably due to stability decrease of less bundled actin fibers in stereocilia (Sekerkova et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current study's model and citations to prior research.

claim: Stereocilia in jerker mice are easier to form tapered structures and easier to degenerate presumably due to stability decrease of less bundled actin fibers.
source: Fitting with this model, stereocilia in jerker mice are thinner in their diameters likely due to loss of Espin1-mediated higher order actin fiber assembly, easier to form tapered structures and easier to degenerate presumably due to stability decrease of less bundled actin fibers in stereocilia (Sekerkova et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current study's model and citations to prior research.

claim: The abundance of Espin is relatively low compared to fascin and plastin in stereocilia.
source: As one of the three known actin cross-linkers in stereocilia, the abundance of Espin is relatively low compared to fascin and plastin (Shin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shin et al., 2013.

claim: Espin may play a regulating role in elongation and widening of actin bundle by concentrating at the tip of stereocilia instead of major structural cross-linking roles.
source: It has been proposed that Espin may play a regulating role in elongation and widening of actin bundle by concentrating at the tip of stereocilia instead of major structural cross-linking roles (Avenarius et al., 2014; Loomis et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Avenarius et al., 2014; Loomis et al., 2003.

claim: The abundance of Myo3 (both Myo3a and Myo3b together) is similar to that of Espin (a few hundred copies per stereocilium).
source: Interestingly, the abundance of Myo3 (both Myo3a and Myo3b together) is similar to that of Espin (a few hundred copies per stereocilium) (Shin et al., 2013), indicating that Myo3 and Espin1 may work together to regulate higher order actin bundle structure formation and stability in stereocilia.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shin et al., 2013.

claim: Myo3 and Espin1 may work together to regulate higher order actin bundle structure formation and stability in stereocilia.
source: Interestingly, the abundance of Myo3 (both Myo3a and Myo3b together) is similar to that of Espin (a few hundred copies per stereocilium) (Shin et al., 2013), indicating that Myo3 and Espin1 may work together to regulate higher order actin bundle structure formation and stability in stereocilia.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from abundance data and the current study's findings.

claim: Stabilization of the growing end of the actin filaments at the plus ends by both Myo3 and Espin1 is a critical driving force for actin filament elongations.
source: It is possible that stabilization of the growing end of the actin filaments at the plus ends by both Myo3 and Espin1 is a critical driving force for actin filament elongations (Avenarius et al., 2014; Loomis et al., 2003; Shin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism based on prior research.

claim: The Myo3 binding-mediated cross-linking of Espin1 cargo is in sharp contrast to the cargo binding-mediated motor dimerization and processivity induction known in a number of other unconventional myosins.
source: The Myo3 binding-mediated cross-linking of Espin1 cargo is in sharp contrast to the cargo binding-mediated motor dimerization and processivity induction known in a number of other unconventional myosins (myosin V, VI and VII) (Lu et al., 2014; Sakai et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with other myosins and supported by citations.

claim: One of Myo3's key functions appears to coordinate with its cargo protein Espin1 to regulate Espin1-mediated actin filaments assembly and stability.
source: Instead, one of Myo3's key functions appears to coordinate with its cargo protein Espin1 to regulate Espin1-mediated actin filaments assembly and stability.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current study's findings.

claim: The study reveals a previously unrecognized direct myosin binding-induced actin bundling activity regulation mechanism of an actin filament cross-linker protein.
source: As such, our study reveals a previously unrecognized direct myosin binding-induced actin bundling activity regulation mechanism of an actin filament cross-linker protein.
evidence: This claim is based on the novel findings of the current study.

claim: The study demonstrates an intimate synergistic action mechanism between two classes of actin binding proteins in controlling actin fiber size and stability.
source: It also demonstrates an intimate synergistic action mechanism between two classes of actin binding proteins, namely actin filament-based myosin motors and actin filament cross-linking protein, in controlling actin fiber size and stability.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings of the current study.

claim: Another unconventional myosin in stereocilia, Myosin XVa, can form a complex with an actin capping protein Eps8 to regulate stereocilia elongations.
source: It has been reported that another unconventional myosin in stereocilia, Myosin XVa, can form a complex with an actin capping protein Eps8 to regulate stereocilia elongations (Manor et al., 2011), suggesting that working together with actin binding proteins to regulate actin skeletal dynamics might be a new mode of function for unconventional myosins.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Manor et al., 2011.

claim: Working together with actin binding proteins to regulate actin skeletal dynamics might be a new mode of function for unconventional myosins.
source: It has been reported that another unconventional myosin in stereocilia, Myosin XVa, can form a complex with an actin capping protein Eps8 to regulate stereocilia elongations (Manor et al., 2011), suggesting that working together with actin binding proteins to regulate actin skeletal dynamics might be a new mode of function for unconventional myosins.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current study and a citation to Manor et al., 2011.
